As the entire project is self produced, Tyler demonstrates complete creative control over the sonic landscape.

So far this album is far less interesting than Flower Boy lyrically. Actually, I'd say this is Tyler's least interesting album lyrically period so far.

The production on this track is really phenomenal. I also really like the actual melody that Tyler's singing on the first verse. The issue is his performance. If someone else who was actually a decent singer sang this melody it would sound amazing. Tyler's voice is just really weak though. It sounds way too amateurish.

The lyrics on this album are definitely starting to get more interesting. The way he's singing about being frustrated by this closeted dude is pretty cool. It sounds like they're secretly in a relationship with each other.
The lyrics are still about being obsessed over someone. He goes on to question whether he's really in control or if he's being manipulated by the person in question, hence the title of the song.
At this point in the album it's clear that Tyler is realizing the relationship he was hoping for isn't gonna work out.
The story is interesting even though it's so similar to that of Flower Boy.

Logic is definitely a better singer than Tyler. I guess that just goes to show how much more skilled Tyler is as an overall artist.

The progression from young punk chaos agent to mature career artist has been so gradual and natural for Tyler Okonma that when Chromakopia arrived last fall, it was not some shock to the system but rather another in a series of auteurist blockbusters.

The gravel-voiced rapper and former provocateur has been carefully sculpting vast thematic statements since Bastard, but with more polish and prestige each go-round, evolving from a disruptor into an accessible/artisanal institution in his own right.
Of course the new Tyler, The Creator album was a meticulously curated audio-visual experience, hi-res and high-concept.
He's spent his whole career riding his own wave, building his own nation-state apart from scenes and trends, and now here he was presiding over it: The king stands alone.

Some of the same touchpoints that have always informed Tyler's work were evident Saturday, be it loudly percussive beats and lightly queasy jazz chords he absorbed from the Neptunes or pageantry and rugged flows that remind me of a time when Kanye West fandom was not just tenable but inevitable.

Those ingredients were part of Tyler's own unmistakable signature sound from the start, so witnessing them within a fancy arena show was comparable to seeing a photo of an old high school acquaintance on Facebook years later, the old recognizable features and immutable personal essence thrust into a new context.
This is a guy who churns out brilliant album-length statements, the kinds of sound-worlds you can end up completely absorbed in.

You could be forgiven for not realizing the awesome creeping horror of 'Nightmare', a swirling whirlpool of David Lynch and HP Lovecraft meet Company Flow sickness, was made by one so young.
It's backpacker hip hop with Southern/horrorcore hip hop and witch house stylings.

If you've heard anything by Tyler before it's probably the Goth Wang anthem 'Sandwitches' (ft Hodgy Beats), which is so cheap and nasty sounding it's probably causing a whole new abyssal depth of offence to analogue synthesizer obsessives.
He is a brilliant rapper. He is genuinely miles ahead in his field. It's just that this is the fairly narrow field of teen nihilism: his medium is getting upset about having to tidy his room.
Distorted vocals and sub sub sub Salem gothic synths and stumbling crunk beats make the first half appalling, mere new nu-metal for lazy mall nihilists.

About half way through the seven minute running time – around the time Tyler utters the priceless line "I'm a fucking unicorn. Fuck anyone who says I'm not" – the track dissolves into limpid-Plaid style electronica with voices intoning gently, "You gotta let 'em go."

For such a supposed badass, Tyler actually spends a lot of this song in exposition mode: "I'm not saying just to go out and do some stupid shit [like] commit crimes." He goes to lengths to explain to young acolytes that his credo is one of self-will, rather than mindlessness.
A fair few of the songs here come in different "parts" or "movements" and it's so long it will try the patience of most but the fanatical. It's backpack rap's Seventh Son Of A Seventh Son.
However, Goblin revels in constantly pulling the rug from under your feet and is actually brilliant in this respect.
But then this is also tiresome late post-modernism taken to its conclusion. There is no objective truth anymore. Nothing can be pinned down to any one meaning.

Tyler is arguably in the same position as regards mainstream hip hop. Clearly not that interested in money and all the other aspirational trappings some rappers stand for, he talks disinterestedly of ignoring emails from the GZA and Plain Pat.

Goblin is art in the same way that Nick Cave and the Bad Seeds' Murder Ballads or Brett Easton Ellis's Less Than Zero are and to deny it such a status, could reasonably be seen as racism. Rather than feeling sorry for Tyler however we should recognize that he's exploiting a loophole more than creating something for the ages. It's 'Art' but it's relatively artless, like Sarah Lucas positioning a kebab on a soiled mattress to look like a vagina, then running an eye listlessly over the column inches that throb in its presence.

Chromakopia is back to that exploratory nature, though this time we're hearing Tyler through a different lyrical lens as he faces a new stage in life.
we are seeing another conceptual turn where the mask on the album cover is more symbolic as he tackles the duality of his person.

"St. Chroma" opens the album by introducing a loop delivered in unison with other tracks, seamless transitions around an elevated core ethos, though inconsistent with the quality of specific elements, specifically, the writing for Tyler, the Creator.

It's an album that wants to be grander in different ways but flunks on hitting high marks because it doesn't lack the skill to bring anything new to the table.
much of that emanates from having a direct vision and delivering it with impact, making the highs stand out more.
It's one of the weaker albums because Tyler, the Creator isn't evolving lyrically despite the mature themes, but that doesn't mean he can't still deliver.
He can give us some resounding depth, and he can flex without being too arrogant and that's why the work feels so well-rounded.

Though I've lamented on how Tyler, the Creator's maturity is so much in the lyrics, it's in the themes, but there are those rare bright spots that allow us to see this new direction, which many know he can command.
It makes me wish there was some more effort into making the production less rudimental, despite having some fun with it himself.
It's too linear and doesn't try to be more than the sum of its parts. Tyler, the Creator is taking a strong step forward as an artist, but there are still things to work on.

One of the more fascinating artistic evolutions of our current generation, Tyler Okonma, better known as Tyler, the Creator, presents us with IGOR, his fifth studio album. After the mutinous, uncompromising sounds of his earlier work (evident in Bastard and Wolf), Tyler's transformation took a massive leap with his use of much richer arrangements, languid grooves, and more considered writing on his 2017 masterpiece Flower Boy.

IGOR represents his sharpest stylistic triumph to date. With the focus more on instrumental layering and texture as opposed to rigid song structure and rapping, the album consists of a smattering of out-of-key synths, dominant piano cords, and one of the strongest bass lines I have ever heard.

The rapping is indeed kept to a minimum — and when he does, his deep, raspy voice is often cloaked in a barrage of digital effects, burying the vocals in a blanket of delicate instrumentals, rather than propping them on top.
Tyler incorporates the vocals of over ten masterful musicians with little chance of the listener guessing where the contributed on the first run through.
I'm used to Tyler building worlds throughout his albums, but there's a universe of sounds in just the introduction to IGOR alone.
IGOR has the twenty-eight-year-old expressing his elegant musicianship, showcasing his strength as a songwriter with a keen eye for detail and musical texturing.

Tyler's continued use of diverse samples on IGOR has further enhanced his insanely unique sound that most fans have fallen in love with, bringing him that much closer to the likes of Kanye when it comes to having an ear for a good sample.
He is the first hip-hop artist in history to achieve a number one album that he wrote, produced, and arranged all by himself.
